Appendix C Information Leakage of Covariant Obfuscation

We formalize the information leakage of covariant obfuscation.

C.1 Auxiliary Lemmas

Lemma 1.

Suppose Y~\tilde{Y} is a normal distribution of nn-dimensional with mean μ\mu and covariance matrix Σ\Sigma. Then

H⁡(Y~)=n2​log⁡(2​π)+12​log​detΣ+n2H(\tilde{Y})=\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac{1}{2}\log\det\Sigma+\frac{n}{2}
Proof.

Refer to Theorem 8.4.1 of [61]. ∎

Lemma 2.

Suppose xx is a random variable on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, GG and HH are two groups, g∈Gg\in G is a random variable on GG following some distribution, and h∈Hh\in H is a random variable on HH following some distribution. The group G×HG\times H acts on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} via x↦g​x​hx\mapsto gxh. Then we have ℐ⁡(g,g​x​h)=ℐ⁡(g,h,g​x​h)−ℐ⁡(h,x​h)\mathcal{I}(g;gxh)=\mathcal{I}(g,h;gxh)-\mathcal{I}(h;xh)

Proof.
ℐ⁡(g,h,g​x​h)\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(g,h;gxh) =ℐ⁡(g,g​x​h)+ℐ⁡(h;g​x​h∣g)\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}(g;gxh)+\mathcal{I}(h;gxh\mid g)
=ℐ⁡(g,g​x​h)+ℐ⁡(h,x​h)\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}(g;gxh)+\mathcal{I}(h;xh)

Thus, ℐ⁡(g,g​x​h)=ℐ⁡(g,h,g​x​h)−ℐ⁡(h,x​h)\mathcal{I}(g;gxh)=\mathcal{I}(g,h;gxh)-\mathcal{I}(h;xh). ∎

From this lemma, we know that to compute the upper bound of ℐ⁡(g,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)\mathcal{I}(g;g(\theta+\epsilon)h), it suffices to compute the upper bound of ℐ⁡(g,h,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)\mathcal{I}(g,h;g(\theta+\epsilon)h) and the lower bound of ℐ⁡(h,(θ+ϵ)​h)\mathcal{I}(h;(\theta+\epsilon)h).

C.2 Upper Bound of Mutual-Information under Group Action

Theorem 7.

Suppose xx is an nn-dimensional normal random vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with distribution x∼𝒩⁡(μ,Σ)x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma), where Σ\Sigma is positive definite. Let GG be a finite group, and g∈Gg\in G a random element of GG uniformly distributed over GG. The finite group GG acts linearly on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Denote the adjoint of the linear transformation g:ℝn→ℝng:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} as g∗g^{*}. Let y=g​xy=gx. Then

ℐ(g;y)≤12[logdet(Σ−1Σ¯)+(μ−μ¯)TΣ¯−1(μ−μ¯)],\mathcal{I}(g;y)\leq\frac{1}{2}\left[\log\det\left(\Sigma^{-1}\bar{\Sigma}\right)+(\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mu-\bar{\mu})\right],

where

μ¯=𝔼g​(g​μ)=1|G|​∑g∈Gg​μ,Σ¯=𝔼g​(g​Σ​g∗).\bar{\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu)=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}g\mu,\quad\bar{\Sigma}=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\Sigma g^{*}).
Proof.

First, we derive the mutual information as

ℐ⁡(g,y)=H⁡(y)−H⁡(y∣g)=H⁡(y)−H⁡(x).\mathcal{I}(g;y)=H(y)-H(y\mid g)=H(y)-H(x).

By Lemma 1, the entropy of xx is

H⁡(x)=n2​log⁡(2​π)+12​log​detΣ+n2.H(x)=\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac{1}{2}\log\det\Sigma+\frac{n}{2}.

Moreover, H⁡(y)≤H⁡(y~)H(y)\leq H(\tilde{y}), where y~\tilde{y} is a normal random vector with the same mean and covariance matrix as yy (the normal distribution maximizes entropy for fixed mean and covariance). It follows that

H⁡(y)≤H⁡(y~)=n2​log⁡(2​π)+12​log​detΣy+n2.H(y)\leq H(\tilde{y})=\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac{1}{2}\log\det\Sigma_{y}+\frac{n}{2}.

Substituting these into the mutual information formula yields

ℐ(g;y)≤12(logdetΣy−logdetΣ).\mathcal{I}(g;y)\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(\log\det\Sigma_{y}-\log\det\Sigma\right).

Note that 𝔼⁡[y]=1|G|​∑g∈Gg​μ=𝔼g​(g​μ)\mathbb{E}[y]=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}g\mu=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu), and

𝔼⁡[y​yT]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[yy^{T}] =𝔼⁡[g​x​xT​g∗]=𝔼g​(g​𝔼x​[x​xT]​g∗)=𝔼g​(g⁡(Σ+μ​μT)​g∗)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[gxx^{T}g^{*}]=\mathbb{E}_{g}\left(g\mathbb{E}_{x}[xx^{T}]g^{*}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{g}\left(g(\Sigma+\mu\mu^{T})g^{*}\right)
=𝔼g​(g​Σ​g∗)+𝔼g​(g​μ​μT​g∗).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\Sigma g^{*})+\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu\mu^{T}g^{*}).

We then compute the covariance matrix Σy\Sigma_{y}:

Σy\displaystyle\Sigma_{y} =𝔼⁡[(y−𝔼⁡[y])​(y−𝔼⁡[y])T]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[(y-\mathbb{E}[y])(y-\mathbb{E}[y])^{T}\right]
=𝔼⁡[y​yT]−(𝔼⁡[y])​(𝔼⁡[y])T\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[yy^{T}]-(\mathbb{E}[y])(\mathbb{E}[y])^{T}
=𝔼g​(g​Σ​g∗)+𝔼g​(g​μ​μT​g∗)−𝔼g​(g​μ)​𝔼g​(g​μ)T\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\Sigma g^{*})+\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu\mu^{T}g^{*})-\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu)\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu)^{T}
=𝔼g​(g​Σ​g∗)+𝔼g​[(g​μ−𝔼g​(g​μ))​(g​μ−𝔼g​(g​μ))T]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\Sigma g^{*})+\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[(g\mu-\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu))(g\mu-\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu))^{T}\right]
=Σ¯+𝔼g​[(g​μ−𝔼g​(g​μ))​(g​μ−𝔼g​(g​μ))T]\displaystyle=\bar{\Sigma}+\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[(g\mu-\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu))(g\mu-\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu))^{T}\right]
=Σ¯+𝔼g​[(g​μ−μ¯)​(g​μ−μ¯)T],\displaystyle=\bar{\Sigma}+\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[(g\mu-\bar{\mu})(g\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\right],

where μ¯=𝔼g​(g​μ)\bar{\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\mu) and Σ¯=𝔼g​(g​Σ​g∗)\bar{\Sigma}=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\Sigma g^{*}).

Further, since Σ\Sigma is positive definite, Σ¯\bar{\Sigma} is also positive definite and thus invertible, leading to

Σy=Σ¯​(I+𝔼g​[Σ¯−1​(g​μ−μ¯)​(g​μ−μ¯)T]).\Sigma_{y}=\bar{\Sigma}\left(I+\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(g\mu-\bar{\mu})(g\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\right]\right).

We now expand the determinant term:

logdetΣy−logdetΣ\displaystyle\quad\log\det\Sigma_{y}-\log\det\Sigma
=logdet(I+𝔼g[Σ¯−1(gμ−μ¯)(gμ−μ¯)T])\displaystyle=\log\det\left(I+\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(g\mu-\bar{\mu})(g\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\right]\right)
+logdetΣ¯−logdetΣ\displaystyle\quad+\log\det\bar{\Sigma}-\log\det\Sigma
=trlog(I+𝔼g[Σ¯−1(gμ−μ¯)(gμ−μ¯)T])+logdet(Σ¯Σ−1)\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\log\left(I+\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(g\mu-\bar{\mu})(g\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\right]\right)+\log\det\left(\bar{\Sigma}\Sigma^{-1}\right)
≤tr𝔼g[Σ¯−1(gμ−μ¯)(gμ−μ¯)T]+logdet(Σ¯Σ−1)\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{tr}\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(g\mu-\bar{\mu})(g\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\right]+\log\det\left(\bar{\Sigma}\Sigma^{-1}\right)
=𝔼g[tr(Σ¯−1(gμ−μ¯)(gμ−μ¯)T)]+logdet(Σ−1Σ¯)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[\operatorname{tr}\left(\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(g\mu-\bar{\mu})(g\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\right)\right]+\log\det\left(\Sigma^{-1}\bar{\Sigma}\right)
=𝔼g[(gμ−μ¯)TΣ¯−1(gμ−μ¯)]+logdet(Σ−1Σ¯)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[(g\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(g\mu-\bar{\mu})\right]+\log\det\left(\Sigma^{-1}\bar{\Sigma}\right)
=𝔼g[(μ−μ¯)Tg∗Σ¯−1g(μ−μ¯)]+logdet(Σ−1Σ¯)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[(\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}g^{*}\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}g(\mu-\bar{\mu})\right]+\log\det\left(\Sigma^{-1}\bar{\Sigma}\right)
=(μ−μ¯)T𝔼g[g∗Σ¯−1g](μ−μ¯)+logdet(Σ¯Σ−1).\displaystyle=(\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\mathbb{E}_{g}\left[g^{*}\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}g\right](\mu-\bar{\mu})+\log\det\left(\bar{\Sigma}\Sigma^{-1}\right).

Since Σ¯=𝔼g​(g​Σ​g∗)\bar{\Sigma}=\mathbb{E}_{g}(g\Sigma g^{*}), we have g−1​Σ¯​(g−1)∗=Σ¯g^{-1}\bar{\Sigma}(g^{-1})^{*}=\bar{\Sigma}, which implies g∗​Σ¯−1​g=Σ¯−1g^{*}\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}g=\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}. Substituting this identity gives

logdetΣy−logdetΣ≤logdet(Σ−1Σ¯)+(μ−μ¯)TΣ¯−1(μ−μ¯).\log\det\Sigma_{y}-\log\det\Sigma\leq\log\det\left(\Sigma^{-1}\bar{\Sigma}\right)+(\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mu-\bar{\mu}).

Finally, substituting back into the mutual information bound yields

ℐ(g;y)≤12[logdet(Σ−1Σ¯)+(μ−μ¯)TΣ¯−1(μ−μ¯)].\mathcal{I}(g;y)\leq\frac{1}{2}\left[\log\det\left(\Sigma^{-1}\bar{\Sigma}\right)+(\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\bar{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mu-\bar{\mu})\right].

∎

C.3 Lower Bound of Mutual Information Under Finite Group Actions

Theorem 8.

Suppose xx is an nn-dimensional normal random vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with distribution x∼𝒩⁡(μ,Σ)x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma), where Σ\Sigma is positive definite. Let GG be a finite group, and g∈Gg\in G a random element uniformly distributed over GG. GG acts faithfully on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} (a faithful action here means the group homomorphism G→GL​(ℝn)G\to\text{GL}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) induced by the action is injective, with only the identity element of GG acting as the identity linear transformation on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}). Let y=g​xy=gx; then

ℐ(g;y)≥KL(δ∥δ0),\mathcal{I}(g;y)\geq KL(\delta\parallel\delta_{0}),

where

δ=max⁡{2​Φ​(ρ)−1,δ0},δ0=1|G|,\delta=\max\left\{2\Phi(\rho)-1,\delta_{0}\right\},\quad\delta_{0}=\frac{1}{|G|},

ρ:=12​ming∈G​‖g​μ−μ‖Σ\rho:=\frac{1}{2}\min_{g\in G}\|g\mu-\mu\|_{\Sigma}, and Φ\Phi denotes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution.

Idea

Regard the map G→ℝnG\to\mathbb{R}^{n} given by g↦g​xg\mapsto gx as an encoding process for elements of GG, and consider the maximum likelihood decoding: the map ℝn→G\mathbb{R}^{n}\to G given by y↦g^y\mapsto\hat{g}, where g^\hat{g} is the maximum likelihood decoder of gg. First show that δ\delta exceeds the accuracy of the maximum likelihood decoder y↦g^y\mapsto\hat{g}; the result then follows via a method analogous to PAC-privacy theory.

To prove Theorem 8, we first introduce the following lemmas:

Lemma 3.

The joint distribution of (g,Y)(g,Y) is GG-invariant, and the marginal distribution of YY is GG-invariant.

Proof.

For any fixed g0∈Gg_{0}\in G, the linear action of g0g_{0} on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} has all eigenvalues with absolute value 1, so the determinant of this linear transformation has absolute value 1. The conditional probability density function of Y=g​XY=gX given gg is thus fY|g​(y|g)=fX​(g−1​y)f_{Y|g}(y|g)=f_{X}(g^{-1}y), where fXf_{X} denotes the probability density function of XX.

It follows that

fg,Y​(g,y)=1|G|​fX​(g−1​y).f_{g,Y}(g,y)=\frac{1}{|G|}f_{X}(g^{-1}y).

For any g1∈Gg_{1}\in G, we have

fg,Y​(g1​g,g1​y)\displaystyle f_{g,Y}(g_{1}g,g_{1}y) =1|G|​fX​((g1​g)−1​g1​y)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|G|}f_{X}\left((g_{1}g)^{-1}g_{1}y\right)
=1|G|​fX​(g−1​y)=fg,Y​(g,y).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|G|}f_{X}(g^{-1}y)=f_{g,Y}(g,y).

This implies the joint distribution of (g,Y)(g,Y) is GG-invariant, and consequently the marginal distribution of YY is GG-invariant. ∎

Lemma 4.

The maximum likelihood decoder ϕ:ℝn→G\phi:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to G defined by ϕ⁡(y):=arg⁡maxg∈G​fY|g​(y|g)\phi(y):=\arg\max_{g\in G}f_{Y|g}(y|g) is a GG-invariant deterministic map.

Proof.

Since fY|g​(y|g)=fX​(g−1​y)f_{Y|g}(y|g)=f_{X}(g^{-1}y), the maximum likelihood decoder can be rewritten as

ϕ⁡(y)=arg⁡maxg∈G​fX​(g−1​y).\phi(y)=\arg\max_{g\in G}f_{X}(g^{-1}y).

It is then straightforward to verify that

ϕ⁡(g1​y)\displaystyle\phi(g_{1}y) =arg⁡maxg∈G​fX​(g−1​g1​y)=g1​arg⁡maxg1−1​g∈G​fX​((g1−1​g)−1​y)\displaystyle=\arg\max_{g\in G}f_{X}(g^{-1}g_{1}y)=g_{1}\arg\max_{g_{1}^{-1}g\in G}f_{X}\left((g_{1}^{-1}g)^{-1}y\right)
=g1​arg⁡maxg∈G​fX​(g−1​y)=g1​ϕ​(y).\displaystyle=g_{1}\arg\max_{g\in G}f_{X}(g^{-1}y)=g_{1}\phi(y).

∎

Lemma 5.

The distribution of g~\tilde{g} is uniform over GG.

Proof.

By Lemma 3, YY has a GG-invariant distribution. Since g~=ϕ⁡(Y)\tilde{g}=\phi(Y), Lemma 4 implies the distribution of g~\tilde{g} is GG-invariant, hence uniform over GG. ∎

Lemma 6.

The joint distribution of (g,g~)(g,\tilde{g}) is GG-invariant.

Proof.

By Lemma 3, the pair (g,Y)(g,Y) has a GG-invariant joint distribution. By Lemma 4, the deterministic map Y↦g~Y\mapsto\tilde{g} is GG-invariant, so the joint distribution of (g,g~)(g,\tilde{g}) is GG-invariant. ∎

Lemma 7.

For any g∈Gg\in G, the decoding error probabilities P⁡(g~≠g)P(\tilde{g}\neq g) are identical, and satisfy

P⁡(g~≠g)=P⁡(e~≠e)=P⁡(∃g≠1​ s.t. ​fX​(g​X)>fX​(X)).P(\tilde{g}\neq g)=P(\tilde{e}\neq e)=P\left(\exists g\neq 1\text{ s.t. }f_{X}(gX)>f_{X}(X)\right).
Proof.

By Lemma 6, the joint distribution of (g,g~)(g,\tilde{g}) is GG-invariant, so P⁡(g~≠g)=P⁡(e~≠e)P(\tilde{g}\neq g)=P(\tilde{e}\neq e).

Furthermore, e~≠e\tilde{e}\neq e if and only if ∃g≠1​ s.t. ​fX​(g​X)>fX​(X)\exists g\neq 1\text{ s.t. }f_{X}(gX)>f_{X}(X). Thus

P⁡(e~≠e)=P⁡(∃g≠1​ s.t. ​fX​(g​X)>fX​(X)).P(\tilde{e}\neq e)=P\left(\exists g\neq 1\text{ s.t. }f_{X}(gX)>f_{X}(X)\right).

∎

Lemma 8.

Let gg be a linear operator on a normed linear space VV, and let x,μ∈Vx,\mu\in V. Then

‖x−μ‖≤‖g​μ−μ‖1+‖g‖⟹‖x−μ‖≤‖g​x−μ‖,\|x-\mu\|\leq\frac{\|g\mu-\mu\|}{1+\|g\|}\implies\|x-\mu\|\leq\|gx-\mu\|,

where ‖g‖:=max⁡(|λ⁡(g)|)\|g\|:=\max(|\lambda(g)|) (the maximum absolute value of the eigenvalues of gg).

Proof.

From the left-hand side inequality, we have

‖x−μ‖+‖g​x−g​μ‖≤(1+‖g‖)​‖x−μ‖≤‖g​μ−μ‖.\|x-\mu\|+\|gx-g\mu\|\leq(1+\|g\|)\|x-\mu\|\leq\|g\mu-\mu\|.

It follows that

‖x−μ‖≤‖g​μ−μ‖−‖g​x−g​μ‖≤‖g​x−μ‖.\|x-\mu\|\leq\|g\mu-\mu\|-\|gx-g\mu\|\leq\|gx-\mu\|.

∎

Lemma 9.

Let the finite group GG act on a normed linear space VV, and let x,μ∈Vx,\mu\in V. For any g∈Gg\in G:

‖x−μ‖≤‖g​μ−μ‖2⟹‖x−μ‖≤‖g​x−μ‖.\|x-\mu\|\leq\frac{\|g\mu-\mu\|}{2}\implies\|x-\mu\|\leq\|gx-\mu\|.
Proof.

Since GG is a finite group, every g∈Gg\in G has all eigenvalues with absolute value 1. The result then follows directly from Lemma 6. ∎

Proof of Theorem 8.

Note that in our case, the probability density function of xx is:

fX​(x)=1(2​π)n​detΣ1/2​exp⁡[−12​(x−μ)T​Σ−1​(x−μ)].f_{X}(x)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}\det\Sigma^{1/2}}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu)^{T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right].

(g​X−μ)T​Σ−1​(g​X−μ)<(X−μ)T​Σ−1​(X−μ).(gX-\mu)^{T}\Sigma^{-1}(gX-\mu)<(X-\mu)^{T}\Sigma^{-1}(X-\mu).

fX​(g​X)>fX​(X)⇔‖g​X−μ‖Σ<‖X−μ‖Σ.f_{X}(gX)>f_{X}(X)\iff\|gX-\mu\|_{\Sigma}<\|X-\mu\|_{\Sigma}.

Hence:

e~=e⇔For any g≠1∈G,∥gX−μ∥Σ≥∥X−μ∥Σ.⟸l​e​m​m​a​9For any g≠1∈G,∥X−μ∥Σ≤‖g​μ−μ‖Σ2,⇔‖X−μ‖Σ≤12​ming∈Gg≠1​‖μ−g​μ‖Σ.\begin{array}[]{rcl}\tilde{e}=e&\iff&\text{For any }g\neq 1\in G,\|gX-\mu\|_{\Sigma}\geq\|X-\mu\|_{\Sigma}.\\ &\overset{lemma~\ref{lemma_ieq}}{\Longleftarrow}&\text{For any }g\neq 1\in G,\|X-\mu\|_{\Sigma}\leq\frac{\|g\mu-\mu\|_{\Sigma}}{2},\\ &\iff&\|X-\mu\|_{\Sigma}\leq\frac{1}{2}\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}g\in G\\ g\neq 1\end{subarray}}\|\mu-g\mu\|_{\Sigma}.\\ \end{array}

Thus, we obtain a lower bound for P⁡(e~=e)P(\tilde{e}=e):

P⁡(e~=e)≥P⁡(‖X−μ‖Σ≤12​ming∈Gg≠1​‖μ−g​μ‖Σ).P(\tilde{e}=e)\geq P\left(\|X-\mu\|_{\Sigma}\leq\frac{1}{2}\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}g\in G\\ g\neq 1\end{subarray}}\|\mu-g\mu\|_{\Sigma}\right).

That is, P⁡(e~=e)≥P⁡(ρ≤ρ0)P(\tilde{e}=e)\geq P(\rho\leq\rho_{0}), where:

ρ:=‖X−μ‖Σ,ρ0:=12​ming∈Gg≠1​‖μ−g​μ‖Σ.\rho:=\|X-\mu\|_{\Sigma},\quad\rho_{0}:=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}g\in G\\ g\neq 1\end{subarray}}\|\mu-g\mu\|_{\Sigma}.

Note that ρ\rho follows the distribution of the absolute value of a standard normal random variable. Thus:

P⁡(ρ≤ρ0)=Φ⁡(ρ0)−Φ⁡(−ρ0)=2​Φ​(ρ0)−1.P(\rho\leq\rho_{0})=\Phi(\rho_{0})-\Phi(-\rho_{0})=2\Phi(\rho_{0})-1.

Therefore, the decoding accuracy satisfies:

P⁡(e~=e)≥2​Φ​(ρ0)−1,where ​ρ0=12​ming∈Gg≠1​‖μ−g​μ‖Σ.P(\tilde{e}=e)\geq 2\Phi(\rho_{0})-1,\quad\text{where }\rho_{0}=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}g\in G\\ g\neq 1\end{subarray}}\|\mu-g\mu\|_{\Sigma}.

Now consider the Markov chain g→(y=g​x)→g~g\to(y=gx)\to\tilde{g}; we have

Consider the deterministic map

d:G×G→{0,1}d:G\times G\to\{0,1\}

defined by

d⁡(g,g~)=1if and only ifg=g~.d(g,\tilde{g})=1\quad\text{if and only if}\quad g=\tilde{g}.

ℐ(g,g~)=KL(fg,g~∥fg⊗fg~)≥KL(d∗fg,g~∥d∗(fg⊗fg~)),\mathcal{I}(g,\tilde{g})=KL\left(f_{g,\tilde{g}}\parallel f_{g}\otimes f_{\tilde{g}}\right)\geq KL\left(d_{*}f_{g,\tilde{g}}\parallel d_{*}\left(f_{g}\otimes f_{\tilde{g}}\right)\right),

C.4 Finite Group Upper Bound

Combine the Lemma 2, Theorem 7, Theorem 8, we have

Theorem 9.

Suppose xx is a normally distributed random variable on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with x∼N⁡(μ,Σ)x\sim N(\mu,\Sigma); GG is a finite group, and g∈Gg\in G is a random variable uniformly distributed over GG; HH is a finite group, and h∈Hh\in H is a random variable uniformly distributed over HH; the group G×HG\times H acts on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} via x↦g​x​hx\mapsto gxh, where the action of group HH is faithful. Denote g∗,h∗g^{*},h^{*} as the adjoint of the linear transformation g:ℝn⟶ℝng:\mathbb{R}^{n}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}, h:ℝn⟶ℝnh:\mathbb{R}^{n}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}, respectively. Then we have

ℐ⁡(g,g​x​h)≤A−B\mathcal{I}(g;gxh)\leq A-B

where

A=12[logdetΣ−1Σ¯+(μ−μ¯)TΣ−1(μ−μ¯)]A=\frac{1}{2}\left[\log\det\Sigma^{-1}\bar{\Sigma}+(\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-\bar{\mu})\right]

with μ¯=Eg,h​(g​μ​h)=1|G|​|H|​∑g∈G,h∈Hg​μ​h\bar{\mu}=E_{g,h}(g\mu h)=\frac{1}{|G||H|}\sum_{g\in G,h\in H}g\mu h and Σ¯=Eg,h​((g⊗h)​Σ​(g∗⊗h∗))\bar{\Sigma}=E_{g,h}((g\otimes h)\Sigma(g^{*}\otimes h^{*}));

and

B=KL(δ∥δ0),δ=max{2Φ(ρ)−1,δ0},δ0=1|H|B=KL(\delta\parallel\delta_{0}),\quad\delta=\max\left\{2\Phi(\rho)-1,\delta_{0}\right\},\quad\delta_{0}=\frac{1}{|H|}

where ρ:=12​minh≠e∈H​‖μ−μ​h‖Σ\rho:=\frac{1}{2}\min_{h\neq e\in H}\|\mu-\mu h\|_{\Sigma}, and Φ\Phi is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution.

Remark 1.

Consider the special case where H={e}H=\{e\}; in this case, we obtain the last (and largest) upper bound of ℐ⁡(g,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)\mathcal{I}(g;g(\theta+\epsilon)h):

ℐ⁡(g,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)≤A\mathcal{I}(g;g(\theta+\epsilon)h)\leq A

with μ¯=Eg​(g​μ)=1|G|​∑g∈Gg​μ\bar{\mu}=E_{g}(g\mu)=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}g\mu and Σ¯=Eg​(g​Σ​g∗)\bar{\Sigma}=E_{g}(g\Sigma g^{*}). In the case of Aloepri, we obtain

A=n−12​log​detCA=\frac{n-1}{2}\log\det C

C=I2​d+1n−1​[σe−1​WembedTσh−1​Whead]​(In−1n​Jn)​[σe−1​Wembedσh−1​WheadT]T.C=I_{2d}+\frac{1}{n-1}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{e}^{-1}W_{\text{embed}}^{T}\\ \sigma_{h}^{-1}W_{\text{head}}\end{bmatrix}\left(I_{n}-\frac{1}{n}J_{n}\right)\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{e}^{-1}W_{\text{embed}}\\ \sigma_{h}^{-1}W_{\text{head}}^{T}\end{bmatrix}^{T}.

Appendix E Attack Success Rate for Covariant Obfuscation

In this section, we focus on the LLM text generation scenario, where X=ℤnlX=\mathbb{Z}_{n}^{l}, Y=ℤnY=\mathbb{Z}_{n} and G=SnG=S_{n}. We consider covariant obfuscation induced by group actions. We follow the idea of PAC privacy [22] and give the bound of attack success rate.

E.1 Static Attack Success Rate

We assume the attacker only holds the plaintext model θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta and the obfuscated model θ~=ϕΘ​(θ)=g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h\tilde{\theta}=\phi_{\Theta}(\theta)=g(\theta+\epsilon)h. The attacker’s goal is to find an approximation g~∈Map​(ℤn,ℤn)\tilde{g}\in\text{Map}(\mathbb{Z}_{n},\mathbb{Z}_{n}) of g∈Sng\in S_{n} such that

g~∘g≈Iℤn\displaystyle\tilde{g}\circ g\approx I_{\mathbb{Z}_{n}}

where IℤnI_{\mathbb{Z}_{n}} denotes the identity map on ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}.

Theorem 10.

Suppose a static attacker recovers g~\tilde{g} by recovering each obfuscated token independently. Then the success probability pp of recovering a single obfuscated token satisfies

KL(p∥p0)≤1nℐ(g;θ~)KL(p\parallel p_{0})\leq\frac{1}{n}\mathcal{I}(g;\tilde{\theta})

where p0=1np_{0}=\frac{1}{n}.

Proof.

Note that we assume the attacker recovers g~\tilde{g} by recovering each obfuscated token independently here, so we only have g~∈Map​(ℤn,ℤn)\tilde{g}\in\text{Map}(\mathbb{Z}_{n},\mathbb{Z}_{n}) (instead of g~∈Sn\tilde{g}\in S_{n}).

For the Markov chain g→θ~→g~g\to\tilde{\theta}\to\tilde{g}, it holds that

ℐ⁡(g,g~)≤ℐ⁡(g,θ~).\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(g;\tilde{g})\leq\mathcal{I}(g;\tilde{\theta}).

Let cic_{i} be a binary random variable where ci=1c_{i}=1 if g~​(i)=g−1​(i)\tilde{g}(i)=g^{-1}(i) (i.e., the ii-th obfuscated token is recovered correctly) and ci=0c_{i}=0 otherwise. Since each token is recovered independently, {c1,…,cn}\{c_{1},\dots,c_{n}\} are i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables with ℙ⁡(ci=1)=p\mathbb{P}(c_{i}=1)=p. Thus

∑i=1nci∼Binomial​(n,p)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\sim\text{Binomial}(n,p)

Consider the deterministic map Φ:Sn×Map​(ℤn,ℤn)→ℝ\Phi:S_{n}\times\text{Map}(\mathbb{Z}_{n},\mathbb{Z}_{n})\to\mathbb{R} defined by

Φ⁡(g,g~)=∑i=1n𝐈⁡(g~​(i)=g−1​(i))\Phi(g,\tilde{g})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{I}\left(\tilde{g}(i)=g^{-1}(i)\right)

where 𝐈⁡(⋅)\mathbf{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function.

Under the map Φ\Phi:

  • •

    The joint distribution fg,g~f_{g,\tilde{g}} is pushed forward to Binomial​(n,p)\text{Binomial}(n,p);

  • •

    The product distribution fg⊗fg~f_{g}\otimes f_{\tilde{g}} is pushed forward to Binomial​(n,p0)\text{Binomial}(n,p_{0}), where p0=1np_{0}=\frac{1}{n} is the success probability of random guessing for a single token.

We then obtain the following chain of inequalities:

KL(Binomial(n,p)∥Binomial(n,p0))\displaystyle KL\left(\text{Binomial}(n,p)\parallel\text{Binomial}(n,p_{0})\right) ≤KL(fg,g~∥fg⊗fg~)\displaystyle\leq KL\left(f_{g,\tilde{g}}\parallel f_{g}\otimes f_{\tilde{g}}\right)
=ℐ⁡(g,g~)\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}(g;\tilde{g})
≤ℐ⁡(g,θ~)\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{I}(g;\tilde{\theta})

where KL(⋅∥⋅)KL(\cdot\parallel\cdot) denotes the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

On the other hand, we have

KL(Binomial(n,p)∥Binomial(n,p0))=nKL(p||p0).KL\left(\text{Binomial}(n,p)\parallel\text{Binomial}(n,p_{0})\right)=nKL(p||p_{0}).

Hence we have KL(p||p0)≤1nℐ(g;θ~)KL(p||p_{0})\leq\frac{1}{n}\mathcal{I}(g;\tilde{\theta}) ∎

Theorem 11.

The success probability pp of a static attack satisfies

KL(p∥p0)≤1n(A−B)KL(p\parallel p_{0})\leq\frac{1}{n}(A-B)

where

A\displaystyle A =12​(μ−μ¯)T​Σ−1​(μ−μ¯)with ​μ¯=𝔼g,h1​(g​μ​h1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-\bar{\mu})\quad\text{with }\bar{\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{g,h_{1}}\left(g\mu h_{1}\right),
B\displaystyle B =KL(δ∥δ0),δ=max{2Φ(ρ)−1,δ0},\displaystyle=KL(\delta\parallel\delta_{0}),\quad\delta=\max\left\{2\Phi(\rho)-1,\delta_{0}\right\},
δ0\displaystyle\delta_{0} =1|H1|,ρ=12​minh1∈H1​‖μ−μ​h1‖Σ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|H_{1}|},\rho=\frac{1}{2}\min_{h_{1}\in H_{1}}\|\mu-\mu h_{1}\|_{\Sigma}.

Here, H1<HH_{1}<H is a discrete subgroup preserving the distribution f⁡(h)f(h); h1h_{1} is a random variable uniformly distributed over H1H_{1}; and Φ\Phi denotes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution.

In this section, we assume the attacker holds the plaintext model θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, the obfuscated model θ~=ϕΘ​(θ)=g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h\tilde{\theta}=\phi_{\Theta}(\theta)=g(\theta+\epsilon)h, and obfuscated user input tokens x∈ℤnlx\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}^{l}. Theorem 12.

The following statements hold: 1. ℐ⁡(g,g​x,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)≤ℐ⁡(g,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)+ℐ⁡(g,g​x)\mathcal{I}(g;gx,g(\theta+\epsilon)h)\leq\mathcal{I}(g;g(\theta+\epsilon)h)+\mathcal{I}(g;gx); 2. The success probability pp of a dynamic attack satisfies KL(p∥p0)≤1n(A−B+C)KL(p\parallel p_{0})\leq\frac{1}{n}(A-B+C), where

A\displaystyle A =12​(μ−μ¯)T​Σ−1​(μ−μ¯)with ​μ¯=𝔼g,h1​(g​μ​h1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\mu-\bar{\mu})^{T}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-\bar{\mu})\quad\text{with }\bar{\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{g,h_{1}}\left(g\mu h_{1}\right),
B\displaystyle B =KL(δ∥δ0),δ=max{2Φ(ρ)−1,δ0},δ0=1|H1|,\displaystyle=KL(\delta\parallel\delta_{0}),\quad\delta=\max\left\{2\Phi(\rho)-1,\delta_{0}\right\},\quad\delta_{0}=\frac{1}{|H_{1}|},
ρ\displaystyle\rho =12​minh1∈H1​‖μ−μ​h1‖Σ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\min_{h_{1}\in H_{1}}\|\mu-\mu h_{1}\|_{\Sigma}.

Here, H1<HH_{1}<H is a discrete subgroup preserving the distribution f⁡(h)f(h); h1h_{1} is a random variable uniformly distributed over H1H_{1}; Φ\Phi denotes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution; and C=ℐ⁡(g,g​x)C=\mathcal{I}(g;gx) is a term that only depends on the length and distribution of the input sequence xx.

Proof.

We first prove the first inequality:

ℐ⁡(g,g​x,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)\displaystyle\quad\mathcal{I}(g;gx,g(\theta+\epsilon)h)
≤H⁡(g​x,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)−H⁡(g​x,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h∣g)\displaystyle\leq H(gx,g(\theta+\epsilon)h)-H(gx,g(\theta+\epsilon)h\mid g)
=H⁡(g​x,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)−H⁡(g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h∣g)−H⁡(g​x∣g)\displaystyle=H(gx,g(\theta+\epsilon)h)-H(g(\theta+\epsilon)h\mid g)-H(gx\mid g)
≤H⁡(g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)+H⁡(g​x)−H⁡(g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h∣g)−H⁡(g​x∣g)\displaystyle\leq H(g(\theta+\epsilon)h)+H(gx)-H(g(\theta+\epsilon)h\mid g)-H(gx\mid g)
=ℐ⁡(g,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)+ℐ⁡(g,g​x).\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}(g;g(\theta+\epsilon)h)+\mathcal{I}(g;gx).

Similar to the proof of Theorem 10, we have KL(p∥p0)≤1nℐ(g;gx,g(θ+ϵ)h)KL(p\parallel p_{0})\leq\frac{1}{n}\mathcal{I}(g;gx,g(\theta+\epsilon)h). Substituting the above inequality gives

KL(p∥p0)≤1n[ℐ(g;g(θ+ϵ)h)+C].KL(p\parallel p_{0})\leq\frac{1}{n}\left[\mathcal{I}(g;g(\theta+\epsilon)h)+C\right].

From Theorem 9, we have ℐ⁡(g,g⁡(θ+ϵ)​h)≤A−B\mathcal{I}(g;g(\theta+\epsilon)h)\leq A-B. Combining these results yields

KL(p∥p0)≤1n(A−B+C).KL(p\parallel p_{0})\leq\frac{1}{n}(A-B+C).

Appendix F Experiment Details

F.1 Potential Threats

Vocabulary-Matching Attack (VMA). AloePri protect privacy by mapping plaintext tokens of private text to obfuscated tokens via a permutation Π\Pi. With knowledge of the obfuscated model weights, attackers can attempt to map each obfuscated token back to its original plaintext token. This threat leverages the Vocabulary-Matching Attack (VMA) proposed by Thomas et al. [25], which is capable of recovering permutation matrices Z1Z_{1} and Z2Z_{2} from the known relationship Y=Z1​X​Z2Y=Z_{1}XZ_{2} (where XX is a known matrix and YY is the observed obfuscated matrix).

The core idea of VMA is to first eliminate one permutation matrix through column-wise sorting, then recover the other one via neighbor matching. Specifically, let RowSort​(⋅)\text{RowSort}(\cdot) denote the sorting operation along each row. it holds that RowSort​(Y)=RowSort​(X​Z2)\text{RowSort}(Y)=\text{RowSort}(XZ_{2}). By comparing the rows of RowSort​(X​Z2)\text{RowSort}(XZ_{2}) and RowSort​(X)\text{RowSort}(X), attackers can recover Z1Z_{1}. Table 8 summarizes weight combinations in AloePri that exhibit a similar structural relationship to Y=Z1​X​Z2Y=Z_{1}XZ_{2}. For AloePri, weights from multiple decoder layers can be used to conduct VMA. Therefore, we adopt a voting mechanism to utilize VMA results of all layers.

Invariant Attack (IA). Obfuscation mechanisms are vulnerable to this attack if they exhibit invariants which remain unchanged during the obfuscation transformation [34]. Based on AloePri’s offline model obfuscation process, we present two types of IAs: Gate-IA and Attn-IA.

Gate-IA: This attack leverages WgateW_{\text{gate}} to exploit statistical invariants. Let 𝒆\bm{e} and 𝒆~\widetilde{\bm{e}} represent the plaintext and obfuscated embedding vectors, respectively. If no noise is added to the embedding layer (αe=0\alpha_{\text{e}}=0), permutation preserves the statistical property of gate-weighted embeddings, resulting in Avg​(𝒆​Wgate)=Avg​(𝒆~​W~gate)\text{Avg}(\bm{e}W_{\text{gate}})=\text{Avg}(\widetilde{\bm{e}}\widetilde{W}_{\text{gate}}). This average value serves as an invariant: it remains consistent between plaintext and obfuscated data. Attackers can use gate weights from different decoder layers to construct such invariant vectors, thereby reversing the token mapping relationship. To defend against Gate-IA, AloePri must add sufficient noise to embeddings by increasing αe\alpha_{\text{e}} so that the statistical consistency of the invariant is disrupted.

Attn-IA: This attack splits WqueryW_{\text{query}} and WkeyW_{\text{key}} into blocks (aligned with RoPE block structures) to exploit mathematical invariants. For analysis, we first ignore the head permutation and block permutation techniques introduced in Algorithms 2. Let Wquery(i)W_{\text{query}}^{(i)} and W~query(i)\widetilde{W}_{\text{query}}^{(i)} denote the plaintext and obfuscated weights of the ii-th attention head, respectively. Define 𝒒=𝒆⋅Wquery(i)=[q1,⋯,qdh​e​a​d2]\bm{q}=\bm{e}\cdot W^{(i)}_{\text{query}}=[q_{1},\cdots,q_{\frac{d_{head}}{2}}], 𝒒~=𝒆~⋅W~query(i)=[q~1,⋯,q~dhead]\widetilde{\bm{q}}=\widetilde{\bm{e}}\cdot\widetilde{W}_{\text{query}}^{(i)}=[\widetilde{q}_{1},\cdots,\widetilde{q}_{d_{\text{head}}}], Q=Wembed​Wquery(i)Q=W_{\text{embed}}W_{\text{query}}^{(i)}, and Q~=W~embed​W~query(i)\widetilde{Q}=\widetilde{W}_{\text{embed}}\widetilde{W}_{\text{query}}^{(i)}. For any block index jj, if ee and e~\widetilde{e} correspond to the same token, the mathematical relationship e(QT[:,j]Q[:,j])−1eT=e~(Q~T[:,j]Q~[:,j])−1e~Te(Q^{T}[:,j]Q[:,j])^{-1}e^{T}=\widetilde{e}(\widetilde{Q}^{T}[:,j]\widetilde{Q}[:,j])^{-1}\widetilde{e}^{T} holds as an invariant. Attackers can iterate over all embeddings to verify this invariant relationship, enabling recovery of Π\Pi. To defend against Attn-IA, in addition to noise addition, AloePri applies permutation over attention heads and blocks to further enhances security by breaking the block-wise consistency required for the invariant to hold.

Internal State Attack (ISA). The attack optimizes input embeddings by leveraging the loss derived from hidden states. Specifically, the attacker first records the hidden states S​t​a​t​e1State_{1} when clients request inference using their private input X1X_{1}. Subsequently, attackers randomly initialize X2X_{2} and feeds it into the pretrained model to evaluate S​t​a​t​e2State_{2}. The attacker can use S​t​a​t​e1State_{1} and S​t​a​t​e2State_{2} to evaluate the loss, thereby optimizing X2X_{2} to recover X1X_{1}. In AloePri, model weights are perturbed with noise and transformation, so that all hidden states during the forward computation process are also noisy and transformed. Consequently, the recovered input data through ISA would differ significantly from the original model input, and cannot be directly used to recover private information.

Inversion Model Attack (IMA). With knowledge of the obfuscation mechanism, the attacker can train a model for embedding inversion [26]. During the training process, the attacker iterates over a public training dataset and generates obfuscated embeddings using the target obfuscation mechanism. With these obfuscated embeddings as inputs, the attacker trains the model to generate raw plaintext embeddings or token indices. In the experiments, we train a Qwen2 model with 2 decoder layers and 8 attention heads to invert obfuscated embeddings to plaintext token embeddings.

Token Frequency Leakage. AloePri applies the deterministic token obfuscation based on the secret permutation. Therefore, an obfuscated text can be regarded as a substitution cipher and still retains the information about the statistical distribution of token frequencies in the plaintext. To investigate how token-level frequency information impacts privacy, we test the token frequency matching attack (TFMA) and the substitution deciphering attack (SDA) [27]. In both types of attacks, attackers attempt to recover substitution ciphertext based on word frequency information from a prior dataset. In TFMA, the attacker uses the prior dataset to count token frequencies, which are then used to match the frequency of ciphertext tokens in the client’s data for token recovery. SDA introduces a recurrence encoding that converts substitution ciphers (1:1 and homophonic) into integer sequences by replacing every unique cipher symbol with an integer symbol standing for its frequency rank. A Transformer-based causal language model is trained on pairs of plain and cipher texts to learn symbol recurrence relations. Then the model is used to translate subsequent ciphertexts to plaintexts.

F.2 Hyperparameter Setting

For all experiments, we fix the generation hyperparameters as follows: temperature = 0.65, top-k = 20, top-p = 0.95, maximum sequence length (max-seq-len) = 8192, and data type (dtype) = bfloat16. Table 9 summarizes the privacy hyperparameters adopted in our experiments, including the noise coefficients for the embedding layer and model head (αe,αh\alpha_{e},\alpha_{h}), expansion size hh, coefficient of the key matrix λ\lambda, and block permutation parameters β,γ\beta,\gamma for attention layers.

F.3 Comparison Experiment

Hyperparameter Settings for Baselines. In the experiment presented in Table 1, we tuned the hyperparameters of the baseline methods and AloePri to ensure a fair comparison. For SANTEXT and RANTEXT, we set their privacy budgets to 33 and 3030, respectively. For DP-Forward, we adopted the LDP mode and set the privacy budget to 55. Additionally, we set the sensitivity to 11. We positioned the noise injection at the hidden states of the 1st decoder layer, thereby offloading the embedding layer and the first decoder layer (accounting for nearly 1B parameters) to the client. Meanwhile, the hidden states were not normalized before noise injection to avoid substantial accuracy loss in the Qwen model.

To reproduce SGT, we trained a 1.6B-parameter model following the Qwen2 architecture, which is used to generate the mean and covariance of embedding noise. This model comprises 2 decoder layers, 8 attention heads, a hidden size of 5120, and an intermediate size of 20480 for FFN. We trained the model on 1M text samples from the OpenOrca dataset and determined the training parameters through grid search. Specifically, we set the learning rate to 3​e−43e^{-4} and trained the model for 2 epochs. We also set the coefficients for accuracy loss, MI loss, absolute cosine loss, and normalization loss to 1.01.0, 3​e−53e^{-5}, 3030, and 1.01.0, respectively.

Benchmark Settings. In the classification task SST2, we fine-tuned the model on the target task using LoRA [62]. We apply LoRA to attention weights and set l​o​r​a​_​r=64,l​o​r​a​_​a​l​p​h​a=64lora\_r=64,lora\_alpha=64. We set the learning rate to 2​e−52e^{-5} for 3 training epochs with a sequence length of 128 and batch size of 64. We evaluated the classification task following the recommended application methods of each method. Specifically, for SANTEXT and RANTEXT, we first obfuscated the training and validation sets using these methods, followed by fine-tuning and inference. For DP-Forward, noise was injected to the outputs of decoder layers in both fine-tuning and inference processes. For SGT and AloePri, we only applied obfuscation during the inference phase.

Generation tasks do not involve fine-tuning or training processes. Thus, in the evaluation of generation tasks, we directly applied obfuscation methods to the inference process.

F.4 Simulation of Mutual Information

We use the Contrastive Log-ratio Upper Bound (CLUB) estimator to simulate the mutual information of both baseline methods and AloePri. In the case of unknown conditional distribution, CLUB simulates the mutual information ℐ⁡(𝔁,𝔂)\mathcal{I(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{y})} between two random variables 𝒙,𝒚\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y} by:

ℐ^vCLUB=1N​∑i=1N[log⁡qθ​(𝒚i|𝒙i)−1N​∑j=1Nlog⁡qθ​(𝒚i|𝒙i)],\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{I}}_{\text{vCLUB}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum^{N}_{i=1}\left[\log q_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{y}_{i}|\boldsymbol{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{N}\sum^{N}_{j=1}\log q_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{y}_{i}|\boldsymbol{x}_{i})\right],

where qθq_{\theta} is neural network-parameterized variational distribution that approximates unknown conditional distributions.

We simulate the mutual information to compare SANTEXT and RANTEXT based on token-level obfuscation, DP-Forward and SGT based on embedding-level obfuscation, and AloePri based on covariant obfuscation. For a fair comparison, we uniformly adopt embeddings for mutual information simulation, where xx and yy in ℐ⁡(x,y)\mathcal{I}(x;y) correspond to the plaintext and obfuscated embeddings after normalization, respectively. Thus, for SANTEXT, RANTEXT, and AloePri, we convert the plaintext token indices and obfuscated token indices to their corresponding embeddings. Furthermore, for AloePri, the obfuscated model parameters θ~\widetilde{\theta} are also known to the attacker, so the simulation target is ℐ⁡(x,y,θ~)\mathcal{I}(x;y,\widetilde{\theta}).
